title: אלישע בן אבויה

paragraphs: Elisha ben Avuya, Avot, chapter 4. He saw Rabbi Chutzpit the interpreter’s tongue (another reading: Rabbi Yehudah the baker’s; Kohelet Rabbah on “Better the end of a thing”; Midrash Ruth on “Stay the night”; Jerusalem Talmud, Chagigah, chapter 2, halakhah 1) being dragged by a pig. He said, “Shall a mouth producing pearls lick dust?”, went out, and sinned, end of Chullin and Kiddushin 39b. His father Avuya was very wealthy in the Temple’s time. To his circumcision feast he invited Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai and his students, Nakdimon ben Guryon, Tzitzit Hakkeset, and Kalba Savua. After eating they went upstairs; Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai began expounding, and fire blazed around the house as when Torah was given at Sinai. Avuya dedicated his son Elisha to Torah. Because it was not for Heaven’s sake, his Torah did not endure. See Ruth Rabbah, Jerusalem Talmud Chagigah, the above Kohelet Midrash at length, and Tosafot, Chagigah 15a. Elisha was one of four entering Pardes (by means of a Name, to heaven; he gazed and was stricken), Chagigah 14. He was called Acher because of an encounter with a woman, who said, “Then he is another,” there 15a. His daughter told Rabbi, “Support me.” He said, “Does his seed still exist in the world?” She said, “Rabbi, remember his Torah, not his deeds.” (Fire descended and singed Rabbi’s bench; he wept: “If so for those disgraced through it, how much more for those praised through it!”) He did not repent, hearing a heavenly voice: “Return, wayward children, except Acher, who saw My glory and rebelled against Me.” When Acher died, they said, “Let him neither be judged nor enter the world to come,” because he sinned. Rabbi Meir said, “Better he be judged and enter the world to come. When shall I die and raise smoke from his grave?” (Yuchasin, in the chronological section: “Although in the pious man’s received tradition he explains Rabbi Meir’s ‘I shall raise smoke from his grave’: while fire burns there is no smoke; pour water to extinguish it, smoke rises and the fire goes out.”) Thus it happened. Rabbi Yochanan said, “Is it a feat to burn one’s teacher? One was among us, and we cannot save him! If I take him by the hand, who will snatch him from me? When shall I die and extinguish the smoke from his grave?” For they would bring him to the world to come without judgment. Thus it was: when Rabbi Yochanan died, the smoke ceased, there, b. Yuchasin writes there, “The main point is that this man never led his students to sin. Even after straying he taught Torah and wanted to benefit them, telling Rabbi Meir, ‘Thus far is the Shabbat boundary.’” But he did not see Jerusalem Talmud, Chagigah, chapter 2, halakhah 1, and the above Tosafot, which say he killed students; see how many he led to sin. See there. The commentator there writes, “He said ‘Thus far is the Shabbat boundary’ to avoid distressing Rabbi Meir; alternatively, to display his wisdom.” End quotation. He merited the world to come through his Torah and students; our holy master also included him in Avot. He saw the destruction and praised Rabbi Akiva; he lived long, being after him. Rabbi Yaakov the tanna was his daughter’s son (see there). Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Yehudah of Kefar Habbavli spoke regarding his words, Avot, chapter 4. When Rabbi Tzadok’s father died in Ginzak, they informed him after three years; he asked Elisha ben Avuya and the elders with him, Mo'ed Katan 20, end of a. See Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Tzadok: the reading differs, having them ask Rabbi Yehoshua ben Elisha; see there. Gechazi was reincarnated in him; because Elisha caused Gechazi’s rejection, he too was named Elisha, Megalleh Amukkot, no.217 [מגע״א רי״ז; attribution provisional].
